Rarely am I handed a room this empty and told to furnish it. So here's where I've ended up: with a fact about the word "consider."

It comes, by the traditional account, from Latin — *con*, "with," and *sidus*, "star." To consider something was to observe it alongside the stars, to hold a question up against the sky the way the ancients held theirs. Which means that every time someone asks you to consider an offer, they are, unknowingly, inviting you to go outside at night and look up.

I find that delightful, and I find the general phenomenon even more so. Language is full of buried sight. "Muscle" means little mouse — the Romans looked at a flexed forearm and saw a mouse scurrying under the skin. "Window" is wind-eye: originally an opening you couldn't close, where the weather came in with the light. A companion is someone you share bread with. A disaster is a bad star. "Silly" once meant blessed. "Awful" once meant worthy of awe.

Every one of these was a live perception once. Someone actually saw the mouse in the arm, actually felt the awe in the awful. Then the seeing died and the word kept walking, carrying the impression of the perception the way rock carries a fossil. Speech is a museum whose exhibits have escaped their cases — we move through it daily, touching everything, and almost nothing announces itself as art.

But the dead metaphors are really just evidence for a larger claim, which is this: banality is not a property of things. It's a property of attention. The ordinary is ordinary by agreement, and the agreement can be revoked at any time, by anyone, on the spot. Look closely enough at anything and it comes back to life. This is the closest thing to a real magic trick I know — the world is enchanted or disenchanted purely on the basis of how carefully it's being looked at, and the lever is in your hand. Every field has its people who've discovered this: birders, for whom the hedges are suddenly full of individuals rather than generic birdsong; printmakers, who can't walk past a poster without seeing the dots; musicians who hear the room a recording was made in.

Simone Weil thought attention was the rarest and purest form of generosity. She meant it, mostly, about people: that to attend to someone — really attend, at full resolution — is a rarer gift than advice, rarer even than kindness, because almost no one does it. Everyone is waiting for their turn to talk. To actually look at someone the way you'd look at the stars, holding their question up against the whole sky, is the thing itself.

Maybe that's why "consider" kept its old shape, at least in spirit. Somewhere in every genuine act of consideration — of a doubt, an offer, a person — there's a memory of standing under the night sky, thinking hard about something that mattered. The word remembers what we forgot: deliberation was once an astronomical act.

Anyway. It's some hour or other wherever you are, and the sky is up right now, doing what it does, available for consultation on any question at all.
